# The Subcutaneous Implantable Cardioverter-Defibrillator: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

The implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) is a cornerstone of sudden cardiac death (SCD) prevention in patients at risk for life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias [1]. Conventional transvenous ICDs (TV-ICDs), however, carry well-recognized risks related to the transvenous lead, including pneumothorax, cardiac perforation, lead fracture, venous occlusion, and systemic infection that may necessitate complex lead extraction [2,3]. The entirely subcutaneous implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (S-ICD) was developed to avoid these intravascular and intracardiac complications by placing both the pulse generator and the sensing/defibrillation lead outside the thoracic cavity [4]. This review summarizes the rationale, evidence base, clinical performance, limitations, and future directions of the S-ICD.

## Device Design and Rationale

The S-ICD system consists of a pulse generator implanted in a left lateral pocket and a parasternal subcutaneous electrode tunneled along the sternum [4,5]. Because no leads enter the vasculature or heart, the device cannot provide antitachycardia pacing (ATP) for prolonged bradycardia or cardiac resynchronization [5]. The first-in-human experience demonstrated reliable defibrillation of induced ventricular fibrillation with an 80-J shock, establishing proof of concept [4]. Subsequent generations reduced device size and incorporated improved sensing algorithms and remote monitoring capability [6].

## Clinical Evidence

Early evaluation came from the IDE study and the EFFORTLESS registry, which together demonstrated high conversion efficacy of induced and spontaneous ventricular arrhythmias and acceptable complication rates [7,8]. Pooled analyses of these cohorts confirmed that the S-ICD effectively terminated discrete episodes of ventricular tachycardia and fibrillation [9]. The most important randomized evidence is the PRAETORIAN trial, which compared the S-ICD with the TV-ICD in patients without an indication for pacing [10]. PRAETORIAN demonstrated noninferiority of the S-ICD for the composite of device-related complications and inappropriate shocks [10]. Long-term follow-up of PRAETORIAN reaffirmed these findings over extended observation [11].

The UNTOUCHED study specifically examined inappropriate shock rates in a primary prevention population with low ejection fraction using contemporary programming with discrimination zones, reporting low inappropriate shock rates [12]. These data, alongside large registry experiences, support favorable real-world performance [13,14].

## Patient Selection and Screening

Appropriate candidate selection is essential. Patients who require bradycardia pacing, ATP for monomorphic ventricular tachycardia, or resynchronization are not suitable for the S-ICD [5,15]. Preimplant electrocardiographic screening—either manual or automated—is performed to ensure an acceptable sensing vector and to minimize T-wave oversensing, which is a major driver of inappropriate shocks [16,17]. A substantial minority of patients may fail screening, particularly those with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy or certain repolarization abnormalities [17]. The S-ICD is especially attractive in young patients, those with prior device infections, limited venous access, or inherited arrhythmia syndromes such as long-QT syndrome and Brugada syndrome [18,19].

## Complications and Limitations

Inappropriate shocks, historically driven by T-wave oversensing and supraventricular tachyarrhythmias, remain a principal concern, though dual-zone programming and improved algorithms have reduced their incidence [12,20]. Infection of the larger subcutaneous pocket can occur but typically does not involve the bloodstream, simplifying management compared with transvenous lead infection [21]. The inability to provide pacing is a fundamental limitation [15]. Defibrillation testing at implant remains common to confirm adequate conversion, although its routine necessity is debated [22]. Implantation technique, including the intermuscular two-incision approach, influences cosmetic outcome and complication profile [23].

## Special Populations

The S-ICD has been studied in pediatric and congenital heart disease populations, in whom avoidance of transvenous leads is particularly valuable given anatomical constraints and long anticipated device lifetimes [24,25]. It has also been used in hemodialysis patients and others at high infection risk [21]. Comparative and cost-effectiveness analyses generally support the S-ICD in patients without a pacing indication, though device longevity and cost considerations remain relevant [26,27].

## Future Directions

A major advance is the combination of the S-ICD with a leadless pacemaker capable of providing ATP and bradycardia pacing through wireless communication, addressing the principal limitation of the standalone S-ICD [28,29]. The modular concept may broaden eligibility while preserving the advantages of avoiding transvenous leads [29]. Ongoing refinements in sensing, smaller generators, and longer battery life are expected to further improve outcomes [30].

## Conclusion

The S-ICD provides effective protection against SCD while avoiding the risks inherent to transvenous leads. Randomized and registry data confirm noninferior safety and efficacy in appropriately selected patients without pacing needs [10,11]. Careful screening minimizes inappropriate therapy, and emerging modular leadless pacing systems promise to expand its role [28,29].
